h: Woodland, a famous plant hunter and the Three Peaks
p: The trail up to the cave owes a lot to Reginald Farrer, the celebrated plant collector who grew up at Ingleborough Hall in Clapham. He brought back plants from his travels in Asia, and some of what he planted still grows along the route today. It's a lovely extra layer to the walk, especially for gardeners, so keep an eye out for unusual shrubs among the native trees.

Above the cave, Gaping Gill is one of the most famous potholes in Britain, a huge shaft dropping into a vast chamber. On certain weeks of the year, local caving clubs set up a winch meet, giving members of the public a rare chance to be lowered into it. If you're a keen adventurer, it's worth finding out when these run, as they're a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

For the cave itself, allow time for the guided tour plus the walk there and back, so a good half day all in. Wear good shoes for the trail, which can be muddy after rain, and bring a waterproof, because the Dales weather loves a surprise.

Clapham sits right in the heart of Three Peaks country, so it's popular with serious walkers tackling Ingleborough, Whernside and Pen-y-ghent. If that's a bit much, the trail to the cave is a perfect taste of the landscape without needing a full day on the fells.

After your visit, take a stroll round the village, with its little bridges over Clapham Beck. Settle and Ingleton are both a short drive away, and White Scar Cave near Ingleton is close enough for a double cave day if you're really keen.
